utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the position is as yesterday, that Judge Robinson is not here, for the same reasons. The position, as we understand it, is that you have a witness, but there are objections to his giving a deposition, which we will hear and see what we can resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure about there being objections to his giving a deposition, because I have just spoken to both my learned friends about Brix Andersen, the witness I imagine you have in mind. Before we come to that, can I mention one other matter and one other difficulty. The other matter is that in certain circumstances -- no, in other circumstances I would have sought an ex parte hearing now, and I think that you probably have been told in general terms the nature of the hearing that I would seek. Ex parte hearings and deposition hearings are covered, if at all, only to a limited extent by authority, and I simply don't know if this Chamber would be prepared, as a two-member chamber, in effectively deposition mode, to deal with the particular part of the ex parte matter at this stage. If yes, then I would ask to have a hearing, and I think it would take about 15 minutes, at most, in addition to the time that would be taken to change all the technical things that have to be changed. If the Chamber is not disposed and doesn't feel that it can deal with that part of the ex parte hearing this morning, then I will take appropriate administrative steps, and we'll deal with that when Judge Robinson is with us again. But it would certainly save time, and a considerable amount of administrative difficulty, if the Chamber were able to deal with just that part of the ex parte hearing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we can't deal with ex parte matters, all that sort of thing, unless we are fully constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand, and I'll deal with that appropriately. The second matter, which is a difficulty, is that Mr. Scott is not particularly well; in fact, he is probably getting worse, and the balance has to be made between the interests of the case and the interests of his health and the health of those with whom he is in contact, either directly or by the air-conditioning. It's always a balance. It may be that although I think he is going to start off this morning, at some stage he will simply have to bail out, and if he does, I hope you understand; I will take over, although I won't have taken the time to prepare the witness because I didn't know this was forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's perfectly understandable, and if Mr. Scott feels he needs to leave, no one is going to complain. Now, what is the position about this deposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me articulate the position from Mr. Kordic's perspective. We have a difficulty in principle with this witness, and that arises from two things. The first is the delivery to us yesterday of the exhibits that this witness is apparently going to authenticate, some 800 pages of these things. Now, we've been able to go through them, but obviously they have not been provided in a language that the accused understands, and that provides a significant difficulty. Secondly -- I've been through this before, and I don't want to be accused of wasting time -- the Court's orders are absolutely clear: All witness statements had to be delivered to us by May the 17th at the latest, after two extensions, and we received a witness statement yesterday, again in a language that the accused does not understand, in English, and apparently the date that that statement was taken was November the 28th, 1999. So we have an objection in principle to this witness testifying as to any of the matters that are contained in the witness statement for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt to understand the position: Have you received no previous witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Now, as a practical matter, Mr. President, we understand that the witness is here; we understand that the Trial Chamber's time is valuable; and, speaking from the perspective of the Kordic Defence once again, we do not object to this witness testifying by way of deposition if the Court -- if the two judges present consider that to be appropriate, with one exception, and that is that as we understand it from the offer of proof that we were given yesterday, this witness is being proffered for two reasons. The first is to authenticate a substantial number of the documents. Obviously, we don't object to that. The second is to offer a wide range of opinions contained in paragraphs 13 through 18 of the offer of proof, and we do object to that, for these reasons: If you take a look at paragraph 19, it's clear that this witness has never met either of the accused and has never spoken to them; and from paragraph 9, it's clear that he's never been to Central Bosnia. So what he is doing is essentially looking over all the documents and coming up with conclusions and opinions of his own, which are built, in turn, upon conclusions and opinions of others who are reporting up the ECMM chain of command that we went into yesterday. So that's the position of the Kordic Defence. We object to his delivery of opinions and conclusions based upon no personal knowledge. We can't conceive of any way in which they would be of any use to the Trial Chamber, and what we would suggest is this: Let's go ahead, do a deposition, and leave the issue of whether those opinions and conclusions -- if the Court feels that they might be of any utility at all, any marginal utility -- leave a decision on the admissibility of those conclusions and opinions until the Trial Chamber is fully constituted. That's our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you have any objection to his producing the documents, as they were? I have just this moment been handed them, but, I mean, the first what I notice is a fax. Is there any problem on this basis, that to some extent these documents are going to speak for themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, two comments about that, Your Honour. Obviously, the witness wrote some of these documents himself and so to that extent he can talk about those. With respect to the other documents, as you point out, they do speak for themselves. They are records of the ECMM and they are going to be coming into evidence and we fully understand them. So we don't have any objection to that. And let me just say, there is a separate subject that we would want to bring to the Court's attention. We had hoped to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, will you slow down, please. Could Mr. Sayers slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- in connection with the confidential witness that was discussed last Friday at the status conference. But we can leave that until the end of the day, if you feel that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So I got your position, you object to the witness's evidence of opinion, or ECMM opinion, as you put it, in paragraphs 13 to 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, between the opinion of the witness himself and the witness being here for testifying, giving the testimony on the ECMM position, I think, as he was head of mission, deputy head of mission in this organisation, he can be able to testify about the position of the ECMM as such, but not giving his own opinion. I think there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I absolutely take your point. I think that creates one difficulty, and let me just say what it is. Obviously, to the extent that the witness has his own opinions or own conclusions, that raises its own set of problems, and we all know what those are. To the extent that he purports to be speaking on behalf of an institution, and giving that institution's opinions and conclusions, I think that raises a whole different category of objections. But more importantly, it puts us in the invidious position of having to cross-examine him on those, and waste time and be criticised for wasting time, when the witness has been proffered, if you like, by the Prosecution as a vehicle for those opinions. Obviously, we would have to evaluate whether those opinions have a valid, factual basis, and I hate to do it, but that's what we have to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, can I just get your position right. You object to the witness producing the documents, in the sense of saying these are the documents, if this is right, collected by the Danish delegation of the ECMM. Now, can there be any objection to his doing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No. That's not our position, and I apologise to the Trial Chamber if I communicated that. I mean, these are obviously ECMM documents, Your Honour, and they do speak for themselves and we assume that they are authentic. So we don't object to the production of the documents. But if I might just summarise, the objection is as follows: First, in principle, because of a violation of the Court's order of April the 1st, which established an absolute right line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am trying to find a compromise here, because we can't make a ruling, obviously, because there are merely the two of us. I am simply trying to find a compromise, to save the time of the Court and also save the time of the witness, to see upon what basis a deposition could be agreed, on the basis that the witness might have to return to be cross-examined or to give further evidence before the Tribunal. If it were possible for him to produce the documents and give his evidence without the opinion part, would you be prepared for him to give a deposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that we would be prepared to give a deposition, provided the issue of late disclosure of the witness statement could be reserved for subsequent adjudication by a fully constituted Trial Chamber. That way the Trial Chamber's time would be maximised, the inconvenience to the witness would be minimised, and the rights of all parties would be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What do you say about his giving detailed evidence or detailed deposition about the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: About the contents of the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would suspect that he should be permitted to do that. We have prepared to examine him somewhat on the documents. Obviously, it's been somewhat hurried and it will be a little disorganised as a result; I hope not too disorganised. But if he wants to give detailed testimony regarding the documents, he should be permitted to do so, so that he doesn't have to be dragged back here yet another time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just thinking aloud. If a deposition was to be permitted or agreed to, subject to matters of admissibility being reserved to the Trial Chamber, you would not object to his giving a deposition, including the production of the evidence, but not giving opinion evidence, paragraphs 13 to 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, that, at the moment, is a suggestion which is made. We'll hear your position on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would agree to an acceptable solution. In principle, I agree with what my colleague Mr. Sayers said, so I don't want to repeat any of it. However, before any definite decision is made, I would like to point out two details. The first is the following: If this witness is primarily supposed to authenticate certain documents, perhaps the witness is not even needed then. At least until now the Defence did not contest the authenticity of any document. If anything was contested, it was the substance, but then we had a live witness who took part in our work, so we could discuss it. That is to say that we are not challenging the authenticity of the documents, we are not saying that various documents were not produced by the signatories concerned, so we don't really need the witness for that. As for the presentation of these documents that come with this witness, we agree that the documents produced by this witness himself be tendered; also, documents in whose creation he participated; and perhaps even those documents that came into his office from the ground. And then on the basis of these documents, if he and his team produced their own documents on that basis, then these documents should be accepted too. However, we cannot agree to having documents that were produced by other institutions and signed by other persons. For example, there are a few documents here that were signed by witness -- I'm sorry, I don't know whether I can use his name anymore, but the witness will be coming in in a couple of days, whose statement we discussed, the one that we are going to take over from the Blaskic case. So I cannot ask this witness about that document because, of course, he is going to say, "I don't know. I haven't produced that document." So I don't think that such documents should be tendered along with this witness. We agree with all the rest. We agree with the most important points. We agree that the Court hear this witness today and then decide on all these objections when the Chamber is here in its entirety. This is only a deposition, but it seems to be a reasonable and a practical solution to me. That would be all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can we make some progress?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. Let me just respond to a couple of points, so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of the underlying documents themselves having not been translated into the B/C/S language, as the Court knows, that's a not a requirement and that has not been a practice. As apart from statements, the documentary materials have never been translated -- the English, French, or what-have-you materials -- into B/C/S. So we don't think there is a firm foundation for any objection on that basis. In terms of the statement not being produced, Your Honour, there simply was no prior statement of this witness. The investigator and I met this witness for the first time on Sunday morning. There was no prior statement whatsoever. Frankly, no prior statement or written statement was required. And I think this -- what this points out is that perhaps leaves us in a position where the Prosecution would like -- would perhaps have been better off not to prepare a statement that could then be characterised as late. We simply could have called the witness without any statement whatsoever. There was no prior statement to produce in March or April of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you may be right, but how does it come about that there wasn't a statement? After all, this is a witness you were going to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be perfectly candid, it was based on an assessment at the time that the witness, this type of witness, with the likely involvement that he had and with the likely knowledge of a broad range of documents, that given his position, that we would likely call. But we had never taken a detailed statement from him before. There had been very limited contact with him in connection with the production of the documents, but it was based on an assessment, Your Honour, that he would ultimately be a viable witness. The outline, Your Honour, that was prepared and tendered to the Defence, again, Your Honour, was to do our very, very best, as we have always tried to do, to provide them as much advance notice as possible. The paragraphs 13 to 18 that the Defence makes particular objection to were simply, again, the absence of a more detailed statement. If you'll accept my characterisation, Your Honours, it's simply a means of putting some very broad statements, as a means of putting the Defence on notice -- on some notice, as opposed to no notice at all, as to what this witness would talk about, and the basic thrust of his statements. They were not, Your Honour, frankly, meant to be exactly the kind of detail outline that we have for most witnesses, because again there was no prior statement or set of statements to summarise. We tried to reach a halfway house, Your Honour, if we could, to simply -- in fairness to the Defence, provide some advance notice of the basic concepts or themes, whatever the Court would like to use, subjects, that the witness would touch upon. And that's the effort that was made to do this. They are not opinions. Most of these, as we pointed out, and as I think Judge Bennouna hit the nail on the head, we are talking about ECMM -- largely here ECMM institutional positions, institutional assessments. This was the deputy head of missions for political matters. He was the most senior official at ECMM charged with these matters and he is in a position to state ECMM's position on these issues. So it's not a matter of personal opinion. Finally, Your Honour, in terms of the documents, virtually all these documents, if they didn't fit within Mr. Kovacic's first and second category, certainly fall within his third category. And that is documents which this witness may have been involved in processing in some fashion. Reports came to him, he read them; he may in many instances prepare other reports on the basis of these reports. There is only, at the very most, very few documents, probably not more than half a dozen, if that many, which might be something different -- a document, for instance, faxed from a third party -- nonetheless received by ECMM and incorporated into ECMM's records. There are few of those. There is, for instance, a statement by President Tudjman that was faxed to ECMM. Well, that's arguably not -- ECMM didn't produce the document, but, as a matter of fact, it's part of their historical records received by them. So these are essentially ECMM documents either prepared, made, or received by them in their ordinary course of business during their mission in the former Yugoslavia, and we think that they are all -- they all should be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The difficulty is that matters of admissibility have got to be dealt with by the Trial Chamber as a whole. So how would you invite us to proceed today? Deal with this, first: Are you proposing to go through this binder with the witness document by document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I had thought to do, Your Honour, last week, before we knew we would be in deposition mode, is there is a big bundle, a thicker bundle of documents which was produced for the purposes of completely covering the documents to be tendered through Mr. Brix Andersen. We didn't intend to go through all of those in detail because, again, of the volume. Then there is a secondary packet, that's somewhat smaller, which we intended to review with him in a more traditional way, although even many of those might be extremely short, by way of just a reference or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see: We have a binder which, I take it, is the larger document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hole punch coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're dealing with these matters, the Court may find it useful to have Exhibit Z2788 in front of you, which is a list of the documents, essentially, and it was tendered to the registry this morning, Z2788.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've just been handed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, let me back up and try again, now that everyone maybe has the materials at hand. This exhibit, Z2788, Your Honour, is a list of what's in this entire thick -- the biggest bundle, with the exception of about two or three documents which were not added until after the list was originally prepared, but it's 98 per cent of what's on this list. And I had a couple of other documents that I intended to supplement with the witness as we proceeded, but essentially, for all practical purposes, these are the same. What the witness is prepared to say is that he has reviewed all these out of court -- it didn't seem a good use of the Court's time to sit here reviewing documents -- and but he would say he's reviewed every one of these documents out of court, as listed on this list and verified by him to be ECMM documents and records. We were going to tender those to the Court, and then there is a smaller packet, represented by this binder, which would be the documents that we would actually, to varying degrees, use in the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the questions of opinion which are objected to, do they appear at all from the documents? Can you deal with them from the documents, as opposed to the witness giving his opinion, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Primarily they come from the documents. What the witness's testimony, in some -- in much respects -- excuse me, Your Honour -- in many respects would be, or is, that he simply -- here is a live witness to confirm that yes, this was ECMM's opinion at the time, but very much based on the historical records. When the Court has a chance -- and I realise the Court hasn't had a chance -- when the Court has had a chance to see the nature of some of these documents, which are contemporaneous assessments by the ECMM in 1993 of what was happening on the ground, you'll see what they are, and they are quite important and helpful documents. But the witness can simply say that -- you know, as the deputy head of mission, "These are documents that we produced, these are analyses and assessments we produced at the time and represented our institutional position."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if the witness gives a deposition, he goes through the documents which you want to refer him to, and he can then be cross-examined on them. All matters of admissibility would be reserved for the Trial Chamber as a whole. It may be that we could make progress on that basis. Mr. Scott, if you are not feeling well and you want to sit down, do so, if it's more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, very much. I'm fine for the moment, but I may take you up on that at some point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that's agreeable to the Defence, we will go on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but could I just make a proposal to make things even simpler: If it is authenticity of the documents, we agree, they are authentic; there is no need to ask a witness about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he is going to be asked globally; I don't think we are going to go through one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've spoken to the legal officer about the formalities, and we would be grateful if the Defence would file their consent again in writing, reserving matters, of course, of admissibility for the Trial Chamber. If you would send in an appropriate document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We will send one over this afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to sit down, Mr. Brix Andersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Brix Andersen, your full name is Ole, O-l-e, Brix Andersen?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you have been a career diplomat with the Danish government since 1973?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You are currently the minister counsellor in the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: I'm a minister counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And how long have you been in that position?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: I've been there in my present job since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is essentially after your return from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, by way of background, sir, that you studied law, and you also spent two years in national military service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: From 1974 to 1976, you worked in the NATO department of the Danish Foreign Ministry, and in fact you attended the NATO defence college in 1982; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your career, sir, you have been posted to various foreign countries as part of your foreign service, including Poland, Saudi Arabia, and China; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: From approximately the 1st of September, 1992, to 1 July 1993, you were the head of the Danish delegation to the ECMM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And from approximately the 1st of January of that year, 1993, you were the deputy head of mission (political) at ECMM's headquarters in the former Yugoslavia in Zagreb, Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, during the Danish presidency of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just for the record, and since it does kind of affect the nature and scope of your testimony, during what period of time did Denmark have the presidency of the EU or EC at that time?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: The first half-year of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in reference to your position, which we will come to again in a few minutes, when it says "deputy head of mission (political)," what were your areas of responsibility? What does "political" mean, in other words?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: There was one head of mission, the Danish ambassador; there was myself, in charge of the political affairs, acting as his deputy, and I would be the acting head of mission in his absence. Then there was a Danish officer, a brigadier general, who was in charge of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was that Brigadier General Villy Durr?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were first notified that you would be posted to the former Yugoslavia during July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And prior to taking up your duties with the ECMM, you took various steps to familiarise yourself with the situation in the former Yugoslavia; you travelled to Zagreb, before -- I think before taking up your duties, to be briefed on the ECMM mission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact you also served as a member of the Danish delegation to the London Conference on the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your posting as deputy head of mission, you were stationed in Zagreb; you travelled to some of the ECMM's regional centres or other offices, but to make it clear, you were not in Central Bosnia during your tenure with the ECMM. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's likewise jump ahead for a moment, just simply make it clear for the record so there is no possible misunderstanding: In the course of your time at ECMM, you did not meet the defendant Dario Kordic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: No, I did not meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you did not meet, ever, Mr. Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, with particular regard to Mr. Cerkez, you really had no knowledge of or dealings with or about him at all; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, turning to your duties, then, as political adviser, or deputy head in charge of political affairs, why don't you tell us a little bit more in your own words about what that job involved and what kind of activities you would be involved in on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: I would review all the reports which came from the field, not necessarily every single of them on a day-to-day basis, but certainly the daily reports which were written up by the operations people and sent to Copenhagen. All of them would pass through my hands before being sent off to Copenhagen. We had a system of sending daily reports, weekly reports, and monthly reports, and from time to time that would be supplemented with special reports if there were subjects of particular importance, either at our own initiative or at the request of the presidency in Copenhagen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that to one degree or another, sir, you had your hands, or at least I can say your eyes, on all of the documents, reports, that were coming through up to the level of Zagreb headquarters and then being passed on to your government? Or if not all --

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Not all the reports coming to the headquarters, but all the reports going from Zagreb to Copenhagen when I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry; I misspoke. Certainly not every report, but you would be the principal officer in Zagreb that would then be involved in compiling reports coming from below, if you will, and then sending on to either the ECMM presidency or your government; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: I would review the draft reports which were presented to me by either the political adviser or the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who were those two individuals, or were they at the time?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Christian Warming, who was a Danish diplomat, and he was in the beginning a Canadian colonel, Noseworthy, who was chief of operations, and he was later exchanged for a British colonel, Ford.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go for a moment to dealing with some document issues. Is it correct, sir, that in the past several days you were presented with a volume of materials, asked to review them for the purpose of verifying if they in fact were ECMM documents or records? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher to please put in front of you both one of the bundles, if we could just have it just for the record purposes, one of the large bundles of documents, and also Exhibit Z2788. Is it correct, sir, that the bundle of documents that's now been put in front of you were reviewed by you and a list was made with reference both to a document identification number and in reference to an exhibit number for the purposes of this trial, and that you were able, in fact, to confirm that all the documents listed in the exhibit marked Z2788 are, to the best of your information and knowledge, authentic ECMM documents and records?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my knowledge, these are original -- sorry, copies of the original documents, and from ECMM, with one exception, which is mentioned in the notes, which is not an original ECMM document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the end of Exhibit 2788, bottom of the second page, there was one exhibit that was characterised, a document that was a bit different. Did you nonetheless recognise that as a document communicated by the European Union presidency to members of governments of the European Union or community at the time?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It has the standard format for such communications.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And beyond that, would it be fair to say that with regard to a number of the documents in that bundle, you would have had more, in fact, more extensive personal involvement in some fashion, either in having actually assisted in preparing or reviewing them, or in some other fashion?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am going to show you three additional documents, Mr. Brix Andersen, that didn't find their way into the bundle. Let's just complete as much as we can this exercise now. Let me direct your attention -- the three that were just distributed. Let me start with Exhibit 939,1, which is a one-page document titled "Meeting at Medjugorje, 18th of May, 1993." And we reserve that document. I think it better in terms of the context, but simply note that you have that in front of you. If you'll go, then, to Exhibit 910,1, Z910,1. Can you review that document momentarily and again tell the Court, is this again an authentic ECMM document or record, from various markings or format that you see on the document?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: From the markings of the document, this is an original ECMM document from the files of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And if you go, then, in similar fashion, to Exhibit Z937,1. Can you likewise tell us, please, whether that is also an ECMM document and record?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It appears, in the same manner, to be a copy from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs files, coming from Zagreb ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I would just say at this point, that represents the scope or universe of documents to be presented through this witness. Subject to the Court's earlier determinations, we -- whatever the Court deemed most acceptable, we tender or introduce or offer those to the Court at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the smaller binder that you have in front of you, and likewise in the smaller binders that the Court and Defence counsel have been provided, these documents should be roughly in the -- hopefully will be in the order in which they will be examined, even though they -- some of the exhibit numbers may be out of order. Let me just alert: Some of the numerical numbering may have been changed because of subject or topic, but they should themselves be in the order which they may come up now in your examination, with the exception again of the three that were loose, which, if need be, we'll address separately. The first Exhibit, then, Exhibit Z707,1. Is this the type of a weekly summary that you -- that was the practice of ECMM to make, this particular summary coming from RC Zenica to, on the title of the document -- on the memo itself, to HQ ECMM?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: All the regional centres were under instructions to file daily and weekly reports, and, as I said, also special reports upon request or their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And sometimes there would be, as I recall, daily reports, weekly summaries, and there might even be monthly reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, the Court has heard some information about these activities or components, but what was RC Zenica? What was an RC in ECMM's organisation at that time?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: The basic structure was that we had the headquarters in Zagreb. Subordinate to that, we had the regional centres, which would then coordinate the activities of what we call the coordination centres, the CC's. And under that there would be the teams. So we would have this structured layer of the headquarters, the RCs, the CC's and the teams. We would go from the teams to the CC's to the RC's, and then they would be compiled and reviewed and condensed and whatever and sent up to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that RC Zenica, or the Regional Centre Zenica, was the principal ECMM office in or for Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as you said earlier, then beneath the RC level there was another -- there were the coordinating centres, or CC, that were even at yet a lower, more local level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the Court just is familiar with the terminology, then, when you see RC Zenica here, meaning the ECMM regional centre in Zenica. Then if we see something like CC Travnik, that would be the coordinating centre located in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: And which would be under the immediate direction of the RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell the Court, during the period of time from approximately the 1st of January, 1993, through the summer of 1993, who was the head of RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: A French diplomat by the name of Jean-Pierre Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit Z707,1, is this a report, a weekly summary from RC Zenica, then, which in particular gives a chronology of various events in Central Bosnia during the previous week?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking to the middle, approximately the middle of the second page, the second one says "comment." A comment is made following the chronology. It says: "All the incidents which took place during the week appear to be originated by one source and been part of a prepared plan. Obviously the provocations were planned to deteriorate the fragile relationships between Croat and Muslims." Et cetera. That would be the type of information, as indeed the information in this document as a whole, which then might be further compiled and reported by you to other senior levels of ECMM, and in fact to the EC; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on to Exhibit 719, which I believe actually has already been tendered, but for purposes of having it all here, we've included it in your bundle of documents. This is something called a special report, and I think you mentioned earlier that in addition to the regular periodic reports, the various ECMM components at any particular time could make special reports of -- which they felt appropriate to make; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. Either at their own initiative or at the request from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And without reading, certainly, the entire document, this is a document that again seems to give a report on various events in Central Bosnia in mid-April 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to Exhibit Z766,1. Can you tell us, look at that and just tell us what that document is and whether you prepared it; and if you did prepare it, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It was prepared in Zagreb for me and for my review, from a meeting which I believe was in Brussels, but I'm not quite sure of that. But it was a meeting of the ad hoc group on former Yugoslavia, and I was asked by the president in Copenhagen to participate in that meeting, and I was asked to introduce the meeting's view on what was going on in Yugoslavia. And it was for that purpose that this briefing paper was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Skipping down to the end of the second page where it talks about Central Bosnia, and going over to actually the third page and the first full paragraph starting on page 3. Was it your assessment at the time, and your briefing, as directed by -- that you were directed to carry out, as you told us a moment ago, that: "The situation in Central Bosnia had deteriorated sharply during last week. A possible explanation for the tension in the area could be the suspected aim of the HVO, while the world's attention is focused on Srebrenica in East Bosnia, to take over the territory of the two 'Croat' provinces. The Muslim community is determined to avoid this. There is a deep mistrust from the BiH side concerning Croat intentions in this region. The HVO is suspected by the BiH to try to 'cleanse' the areas around Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, Travnik, Prozor, Vitez and Busovaca." Was that assessment reached on the reports you were receiving from the field and that became part of the analysis and assessment in the headquarter's office in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. This is based on the reports we received from mainly RC Zenica, and it was based on the assessment with that in headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit Z812,1. Is it correct, sir, this is then a weekly summary for the week of the 17th, the 24th of April, 1993, from RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking to the second paragraph under the title "Summary." Was it the report that it was the clear position of CRO -- is that an abbreviation for Croat, Croatian?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "... clear position of CRO authorities to implement the Vance-Owen Plan, pressing the Muslim population to leave the so-called 'Croat provinces,' provoked their reaction, with very strong and cruel fighting and actions against the civilian population." And the rest of the memo goes on to talk about essentially these matters in greater detail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the last paragraph starting on the next page. The report states that: "The Croatian community and authorities at all levels consistently quote the Vance-Owen Plan, and HVO will implement the plan without delay, and by force, if necessary. This policy is dangerous and has resulted in a Muslim backlash through Central Bosnia and Mostar, where provocation has been extreme." Was it the assessment of the ECMM during this period, sir, that there had been, in the first part and mid-April of 1993, an organised offensive or campaign carried out by the HVO against various Muslim towns, villages, locations in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. That was our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you understand this -- if any, the connection between this series of attacks or campaign and the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, at least the implementation in the views of one group, that is, the Croats?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: I didn't get the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you understand there to be any connection between this series of attacks in mid-April 1993 and the implementation or carrying out of the Vance-Owen Plan, at least as that plan was interpreted by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It was our assessment that the Croat leadership used the Vance-Owen Plan as a vehicle for gaining control of what was assigned as provinces 8 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue on to Exhibit 840. I simply want to point your particular attention to the bottom of the second page. There is a paragraph or a section starting "40 trucks, UNHCR convoy." It was reported to you, or to the Zagreb office, by the head of RC Zenica at the time, which again was Mr. Thebault, that: "A 40-truck convoy of food supplies escorted by two warriors was hijacked on its way to Zenica. The HVO forces responsible for this action claimed that they did not care of the orders of Colonel Blaskic and Brigadier Petkovic concerning the free movement, that they had strict orders from Mr. Kordic, official highest-level representative of HVO for Central Bosnia, to arrest this convoy and to search it. BritBat decided to send immediately a company of warriors to have the convoy back. I --" "I" again referring to Mr. Thebault. "-- took Brigadier Petkovic outside of the meeting and stressed the absolute craziness of this action of the HVO, which was a deliberate provocation against UNPROFOR concerning the core of its mandate." "He," meaning apparently Mr. Petkovic, "decided to reach Mr. Kordic, and, after several telephone calls, succeeded in obtaining from him the release of the convoy." Is that part of the report that you received from Mr. Thebault, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, the document speaks for itself. We are going to be wasting a huge amount of time here if we are just going to go through these documents, have pieces read out, and then have the witness [sic] say, "Is that what the document says?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, except for this: that the relevance of the documents can be pointed out. It seems to me the Prosecution are entitled to do that; otherwise it's just a pile of documents. And it is useful for them to say what they rely on. Of course, the cross-examination about the documents, or the foundation for the documents, must come from another witness, which can be dealt with in due course, and you won't be expected to cross-examine, of course, on these matters about which this witness knows nothing except what was reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in regard to that, Your Honour, it is certainly our intention to, if you will, pick up some speed as we go; but as the Court has indicated, we would like to point out some of the more relevant passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've been reminded also, sir, again, for both of us, if we can pause between question and answer, it makes it easier for the interpreters. Now, I'm going to point you to another part of this memo down the page, but before I do so, can you state in your own words the assessment, if any, that ECMM had of a man named Dario Kordic, and where he fit within the events in Central Bosnia or the Bosnian Croat leadership?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: As I stated a little while ago, I have never met Mr. Kordic, never had any dealings with him in writing, so my knowledge of him is from the documents, from the reports, mainly from RC Zenica. Based on these reports, it was the assessment of ECMM, and my own opinion, that Mr. Kordic had an influential position, in some areas a controlling position, within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you know, or again, was it part of the ECMM's assessment, whether Mr. Kordic had any particular relationship to Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. It was reported to us that he was a relative of Mr. Boban, a cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from any family relationship, in terms of their working or political or governmental relationship, what, if any, understanding did ECMM have between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: The assessment in Zagreb was, again, based on the reports which reached us, that they worked closely together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention, then, to one of the paragraphs under item 4, "Comment," again, it was reported to you that Mr. Kordic is in fact "the cousin of Mr. Boban, his special delegate in Central Bosnia, and located in Busovaca, the main responsible" -- and I'll just leave it at that, I suppose, whether it's "the main responsible" something or "the man responsible" -- "identified by all agencies of the troubles in Busovaca two months before and again today." And then he essentially repeats the story about the convoy, saying that it could only be released on Mr. Kordic's special orders. "It is absolutely needed to put pressure on him immediately." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It's correct that this was reported to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And not only reported to you, but accepted, and, if true -- and that's the question to you -- was that incorporated and became part of the ECMM's assessment of what was happening in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Object to the leading nature of that question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, sir, what role, if any, this information played in ECMM's reaching its positions or making its overall assessments in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It entered into our assessment on what was going on in Central Bosnia. It didn't have -- what shall I say -- operative effects, for what happened in headquarters, in the sense that we would initiate dealings with Mr. Kordic from the headquarters in Zagreb. These dealings we would leave to RC Zenica. We would report it further on the chain of command up to the president in Copenhagen, but it is not my recollection that we had any dealings at all with Mr. Kordic from the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And that was left primarily to Mr. Thebault and his staff?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on to Exhibit Z859,1. Directing your attention to the last page of the exhibit momentarily, this in fact again is a report prepared by Mr. Thebault, and if not signed, but at least initialled off by him, "Best regards, Jean-Pierre Thebault"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you find in your working relationship with Mr. Thebault, in terms of -- did you find the reports coming from RC Zenica to be competent and reliable reports?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It was our assessment in Zagreb that Jean-Pierre Thebault was probably one of the best heads of a regional centre we had, and had had for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll tell the Court that this is a particularly rich document, but I will only, for present purposes, point Mr. Brix Andersen to two paragraphs, but -- well, the document, as we say, speaks for itself; but there is a tremendous amount of material in this particular document that I would call to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, would you look at the last paragraph on the second page of this document, starting with "All of this."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to what we talked about yesterday, for instance, we shall not be able to cross-examine the witness about the document, because he was not prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since the documents are being produced, let it be done now, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: (redacted). All this witness is doing is simply producing the document for what it's worth. He can't take the matter any further. Really, the only significance of pointing out passages is that there may be relevant matters which, clearly, the Prosecution want to rely on, and they're entitled to point them out. (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing, Mr. President: (redacted) (redacted) I'm afraid this will affect our interests. What will happen, and it has happened several times, that we were anticipating there were witnesses and refrained from certain questions or from certain submissions, and then those witnesses did not come, or the Prosecution decides not to call them after all, and then we're left high and dry. So this is a practical problem, really, that I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, but let us cross the bridge when we come to it. If the other witness doesn't appear, then we would have to consider the admissibility of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Brix Andersen, at the bottom of the second page -- again, only directing your attention to a couple of particular paragraphs -- this particular paragraph was reported by Mr. Thebault that "All this," meaning the events reported above, "All this has been closely monitored in Central Bosnia by direct HVO high-level commissioners, M." -- perhaps "Mr.," or what have you -- "M. Dario Kordic, Mate Boban's cousin and 'minister for Herceg-Bosna,' located in Busovaca, since the beginning of the troubles there; M. Anto Valenta, HVO vice-president, located in Travnik, where he took a decisive part to the recent troubles just before the conflict; M. Ignjac Kostroman, general secretary of HVO travelling the area." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, and I think I can explain the M's. Mr. Thebault is a Frenchman, so that would stand for "Monsieur."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was about to suggest that myself, but thank you. Going to the next page, the second paragraph under item 2 -- and I will ask you to comment on this beyond the document, if you are able to -- the document itself says, "The political pressure put last week on Croatia was fruitful but not powerful enough. It maybe helped to stop the large-scale military actions, in particular in prohibiting, at least for the while, the large-scale involvement of the military forces of Croatia in order to 'defend the Croat community against the Muslim extremists.'" Based on your role as deputy head of mission, political affairs, can you explain to the Court why putting political pressure on Croatia would be connected to events in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was the assessment of the ECMM, chaired by the president in Copenhagen, that there was a close link between the Bosnian Croats and the state of Croatia, and that in order to influence events inside Bosnia, you would have to rely also on pressure being put on the leadership in Zagreb, which actually also did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that during your tenure, a number of occasions on which direct high-level international communications, if you will, were made to the Zagreb government, and in particular to President Tudjman himself, in connection with that government or Mr. Tudjman using their position or role to affect affairs in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Without being able to give you the specific dates, pressure was being put to bear by the co-chairmen, Vance and Owen, by the presidency, on Mr. Tudjman and the government in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue on, then; Exhibit 910. When you look at -- this is a little bit different than the weekly summaries or reports that we've been seeing before. Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: The document in Danish is just a cover note sending the report of the three ambassadors to Copenhagen, suggesting that it be sent out as a COREU, as it is called, which is an acronym for the communication between the presidency and the other European union capitals, which is used for political, consular, et cetera, affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So apart from the cover communication itself, we have then an enclosed report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what this report was? And I'm not sure this has been brought to the Court's attention before, but what was this effort about?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Apart from the mission leadership as such, which was controlled by the presidency, there was also national contingents, with each having a head of delegation. These heads of delegation would meet with the mission leadership a couple of times a week, during the Danish presidency, to discuss the situation and to recommend whatever action perhaps needed to be taken in capitals, of either a political nature or logistics, getting more monitors, getting more funds, getting more radios or vehicles or whatever. But this was a useful committee discussing these issues. Now, in that committee, the idea was brought up to do something at a fairly high level, and fairly visible on the part of the ECMM, in order to investigate what had been done in Ahmici and to get a broader perspective on what was going on in Central Bosnia. This was not in order to undermine the efforts of Mr. Thebault, but it was in order to be certain that the assessments we were making in Zagreb on the basis of the reports from RC Zenica would also stand up to verification. It was therefore decided to send the three heads of delegation from Britain, France, and Spain, on a joint mission to the area in order to see for themselves and to report back to headquarters. And that is their report here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Leaving, again, most of the document to speak for itself, let me simply direct your particular attention to paragraph 13, on the -- well, what's numbered, in handwriting, page number 4 in the upper right corner. And at the end of paragraph 13, under "Conclusions," did this delegation, made up of the head of -- this essentially fact-finding mission, made up of the heads of the British, French, and Spanish delegations, conclude that these events had not been so much "as a result of the actions of uncontrolled elements, but rather as a result of the application of deliberate HDZ/HVO policy"?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: As it says in the document, that was their assessment, and this was an assessment which was discussed in Zagreb and accepted by the rest of the delegations and by the mission leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on, then, to Exhibit Z926 and touch on it only momentarily. The Court has seen this document before. Was one of the ECMM staff in Zagreb at this time, working with or for you, a man named Charles McLeod?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Charles McLeod was at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in addition to this other mission, was Mr. McLeod sent on a similar investigative mission, if you will, concerning the events in Central Bosnia in mid-April 1993?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as reflected only in part here, not to -- for the purpose of not reproducing the entire document, Mr. McLeod did in fact make a written report back to ECMM headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. He was a very meticulous person, so he made a fairly long report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your general view or assessment of Mr. McLeod's work and competence?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: He was a very competent monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've already had this document produced, and Mr. McLeod has given evidence about it, so I don't think there is any point in going over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly the end of it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That might be a convenient moment to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I've been asked by the interpreters to slow you down in reading the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They have apparently got them, but it's difficult to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Brix Andersen, if we could continue with Exhibit 9. I should correct this, Your Honour. It's now been clarified that 936,1, Your Honour, that number was previously signed, so if the Court will allow us to redesignate this exhibit, and the Registry, please, as 936,3. In any event, Mr. Brix Andersen, only one highlight on this particular document, which is a report from Mr. Thebault concerning freedom of movement. About the middle of the first paragraph, it was in Mr. Thebault's report and ECMM's assessment that: "The blocking of the two or three roads leading to Central Bosnia, and therefore to Tuzla, areas where most of the Muslim population is now living, is one of main HVO policy." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise. I said: Was it Mr. Thebault's report and ECMM's assessment, as reported by -- stated by Mr. Thebault in the middle of that first paragraph, that: "The blocking of the two or three roads leading to Central Bosnia, and therefore to Tuzla, areas where most of the Muslim population is now living, is one of the main HVO policy."

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. It was our assessment that the HVO, they tried to do whatever they could to block the convoys, and they used quite a lot of resources in this end to try to see how to get the convoys through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you on some general topics, before we turn to the next document. Can you tell the Court, to the extent that you may or may not have touched on it already, what was the ECMM's assessment of the position or desire of the HVO and Herceg-Bosnia leadership to have the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna come into any sort of formal relationship with the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It was our assessment that the Croats in Herceg-Bosnia, they wanted a confederation or federation, or whatever kind of relationship, with Croatia, meaning, in effect, that they would be living in a -- not perhaps a unitary state, but in a state for Croats, so that there would be a stronger link between Herceg-Bosnia and Croatia than there would be between the Bosnian Croats and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it ECMM's assessment whether there was any sort of overall concept or strategy of how the Herceg-Bosnia and HVO leadership would accomplish this? Let me rephrase that. Was it ECMM's assessment that there was such an overall concept or strategy?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. That was our assessment, that it was a concept and a strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court any assessment or conclusions that the ECMM reached in terms of whether, among the Herceg-Bosnia and HVO leadership, there was any policy or strategy, at that level, involving ethnic cleansing directed against Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It was our assessment, through 1993, and the first half-year when I was there, that there was a policy of ethnic cleansing directed against the Muslims in order to have a -- to have provinces 8 and 10 predominantly, or almost exclusively, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You have touched upon, I think, the existence of ties between the government of Republic of Croatia and Herceg-Bosnia. What was ECMM's assessment of the level of support that Zagreb showed toward the Herceg-Bosnia, HVO leadership, in connection with that leadership's aspirations to be confederated with or joined with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It was our assessment, and I believe it was shared by the member governments of the European Union, that there was a strategy of support by the Croatian government to the leadership of Herceg-Bosnia. From our reports, which we will come to, it will appear that we were looking very carefully for evidence of this. It was difficult to establish evidence of direct Croatian HV involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there were many signs that the Croatian government actually supported Herceg-Bosnia and the Bosnian Croats politically, with equipment and with troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard, then, let's go forward to Exhibit Z1012. This is a report from the deputy head of RC Zenica, which I believe is the reference to DHRC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in June, 1993, do you recall whether that was Mr. Bees?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was Mr. Bees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This memo is directed, in part, to you as "DHOM (political ops)"?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: When it is addressed to "DHOM (political ops)," that means that it goes to both political: myself; and operations, General Durr.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A few highlights under item 2: "The existence and extent of HV involvement has always been difficult to define, and the many reports provided by the BiH armija have seldom been confirmed by ECMM, UNMOs or UNPROFOR." And that is consistent, in fact, with your testimony a moment ago; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. Of course, the embarrassment value would be high if we could find out evidence of HV involvement inside Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were looking for it. It was not the action of the individual team, or team leader, to try and find at his own will. It was the mission policy to try and see to what extent there would be Croatian involvement. Like on the other side, there would be similar resources deployed, or attempted to be deployed, to try and find involvement by the Yugoslav army on the Bosnian Serb side. So we were always on the lookout for evidence of outside interference in the affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You started out in your answer just now, and you said, "To find such evidence would have had a high embarrassment value." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: It was our assessment that Croatia did provide such assistance, to a higher or lesser extent, but we were fairly confident that that was actually what was taking place. Now, the pressure which had been brought to bear on the Croatian government indicates that that was a combined assessment, not only of the ECMM, but also of capitals. In that respect, it should be borne in mind that all the daily reports, the weekly reports, the monthly reports, were not only sent to Copenhagen, but they were sent, distributed by Copenhagen, to all the member countries. And had we been widely off the track, I'm fairly confident that other member governments would have indicated to the presidency that they should bring us under control. That did never happen. We never had any instruction from Copenhagen indicating that we were off the mark in this respect, trying to find evidence of Croatian involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two other --

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: And I can add to that, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: -- that we were in daily contact. Perhaps not every single day, but I would, several times a week, consult on the telephone with the desk officers in Copenhagen about what was going on in the mission area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A couple of additional highlights. Under item number 5, and simply the first part of that paragraph: "It is not in the interest of either party for HV troops to be seen in Bosnia, and in practice, with good planning, there is much that can be done to hide their activity." And then it goes on to describe that in more detail. You indicated that this wasn't just something that was left to the individual monitors, but that it was ECMM's institutional position to try to document the HV involvement to the extent possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, on the very end of the document, it concluded that "Evidence for HV involvement exists. It has had a considerable impact on the military balance in favour of the HVO and shows no sign of ceasing." Let me direct your attention next to Exhibit Z1050.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where am I going to find this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- I had difficulty with 1012.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I should -- it should be there. There's two maps -- I'm sorry. There are two maps that are part of Exhibit 1012, and then there should be a divider sheet, and then there should be 1050, I hope, in the yellow -- in the manila binder. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't have it, but I've just been handed 1050. Perhaps we could have a copy of 1012, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On Exhibit Z1050, again, a report concerning HV involvement in BiH -- well, let me direct your attention for now just to the second -- it's hard to say exactly the number, but it's approximately the middle paragraph, saying "Regardless." You touched on earlier, sir, that there were a number of instances in which pressure -- or whatever term might be better -- diplomatic efforts were made toward the government of Croatia to intercede with the Bosnian Croats to stop or control events in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. But if you allow me, on this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: -- to make the comment that this is not a report from the field; this is a report prepared at headquarters and sent and copied to RC Zenica. As you will see, it is from headquarters ECMM info section.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: So this is based on headquarters' assessment of the situation, talks with UNPROFOR, talks with other sources. So it is not a report from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, at the bottom of the page, the name "Hal Pugh" appears. Who was he, or what position did he have? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: He was a monitor serving in what was called the info section, which would in practice gather information on the forces on the ground and other information which would be relevant to the teams to know, so that to the extent that we had knowledge from other sources, in Zagreb, we would take care to distribute that information to the teams for their security and for their interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. In reference to the paragraph under -- it's under "Beginning text," or "Begin text," did you recall or have any knowledge at the time of this conversation with the HV Major-General Praljak about HV involvement in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Seeing the document now, I have a vague recollection that this conversation took place. I did not take part in it myself, and as I said, it's only a vague recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: This would be consistent with the efforts of the mission to try and limit the outside interference into events in Central Bosnia. But as I said, I have no personal knowledge of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the second -- in the -- I'm going to call it the third paragraph, again, the paragraph starting with "Regardless"; at the end of that, it states that "Indeed, there are some indications that Croatia has taken heed of warnings from the international community about involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Can you assist the Court with any instances that you can recall now as to what might have indicated in fact that Croatia was heeding warnings? Do you know of any steps that Croatia or its government took to intercede in the events in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN
utterances.text: Like I said just before, it was always difficult for us to follow events on the ground because most of the movement of troops, equipment, et cetera, would take place at night or in areas where we had little or no access. From time to time some areas would be declared off limits to ECMM and to UNPROFOR, which in certain cases indicated to us that something was going on which we were not supposed to see. So the assessment here is based on impressions, from the various people involved, of talks with the Croatian government or President Tudjman. This could be the co-chairmen of the conference, Lord Owen and Mr. Vance; it could be EU ministers, European ministers, meeting with the Croatian leadership in Geneva, in New York, other places. It could be the result of communiqués issued by the European Union, but the combined assessment was, as stated here, that there was actually some effect of the pressure which the European Union and others wanted to bring to bear on Croatia. But it's difficult to quantify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Will you go on, please, then, to Exhibit Z1151,1. Following up on the last question, toward the bottom of the second page of that exhibit: "A last strong protest of the international community against HV involvement has probably had an effect and lead HV and the HVO to a very strict and cautious attitude. It is so no more possible to deny a certain level of HV troop involvement after several months of observation, although it still remains difficult to estimate accurately its scale."
